meaning.evidence: Every beat survives: the '49/'50 hedge, the flume, betting either side, the straddle-bug to Mexico, the parson's wife, the fifteen-minute nag. Additions hang off the original: "Talk about a one-track mind." and "Wheezin' like a busted bellows, and still she'd get up." are reactions, not new facts.

sense.evidence: Terms fit: "cashed up or you'd find him stony broke" for flush/busted, "chook-fight", "properly crook" for sick, "a fair bit of dosh". "go off like a frog in a sock" fits the mare's frantic finish. "how long it was on the frog and toad" carries 'on the road' correctly, if a touch quaint.

authenticity.evidence: Mostly natural Aussie laid over the old dialect: "happy as", "a lucky bugger", "a skerrick of difference", "slow as buggery". The rhyming slang "on the frog and toad" is the one stock-feeling line; "strewth" is a little stagey but in place of "why".

register.evidence: A full yarn voice with plenty of slang ("he'd bet on any bloody thing", "slow as buggery"), but much of Twain's frame is kept as-is ("the curiousest" becomes "the most curious feller", "uncommon lucky"), and it stays at bugger/bloody where vulgarity 2 was available. Slightly under level 5.

tone.evidence: The deadpan, rambling tall-tale tone holds; the punchline "'Well, I'll resk two-and-a-half she don't, anyway.'" lands, and the narrator's earnestness about Parson Walker ("a decent bloke into the bargain") stays.

flow.evidence: Reads aloud easily as one long breathless yarn; elisions like "bettin' on anythin' that come along you ever seen" sit naturally. The closing tag "Wheezin' like a busted bellows, and still she'd get up." is a slightly awkward add-on.

variety.evidence: Varied: "bloke", "feller", "bugger", "dosh", "skerrick", "crook", "strewth", "happy as"; "ya" recurs but not to the point of a tic.

essence.evidence: Unmistakably Twain's Simon Wheeler: the digressive run-on sentences, the dialect spellings "solit'ry", "inf'nite", "Prov'dence", "m-o-r-e dust" all retained under the Aussie.

problems.quote: how long it was on the frog and toad
problems.original: how long he was on the road
problems.why: Rhyming slang reads as a stock Aussie-ism dropped in; plain 'on the road' or 'on the track' would sound more natural.

problems.quote: Wheezin' like a busted bellows, and still she'd get up.
problems.why: Added tag; 'get up' (win) is apt, but the line repeats the finish just described and slightly blunts the paragraph's ending.

problems.quote: strewth, if there was two birds sittin' on a fence
problems.original: why, if there was two birds setting on a fence
problems.why: 'Strewth' as a drop-in for 'why' is a little stagey.

A.summary: A faithful, lively Aussie retelling that keeps Twain's dialect and rhythm; slightly under the brief in weight and vulgarity, with a couple of stock touches.

meaning.evidence: Most content survives verbatim, but some lines are changed: "a good man" becomes "a dead-set legend, mate"; "before he thought" becomes "before he reckoned"; insults the listener with "he'd change sides, ya flamin' mongrel".

sense.evidence: Several wrong-sense swaps: "stoushn't" (a garbled 'warn't' turned into stoush, a fight), "she get rapt'n desperate" (rapt means delighted, not excited), "before he reckoned" (reckon is to opine, not to stop and think), "a dead-set legend" for a good, pious man.

authenticity.evidence: Stock phrases are bolted on: "Fair dinkum,", "Crikey,", "Jeez,", "cobber.", "Stone the flamin' crows." No Australian would call the listener a "flamin' mongrel" mid-sentence for no reason.

register.evidence: Slang density is roughly level 5 by count, but it is sprinkled onto an otherwise untouched original ("which he judged to be the best exhorter about here"), and "for a fuckin' good while" puts swearing where it jars. Weight is uneven rather than off on average.

tone.evidence: The deadpan is broken: "for a fuckin' good while" about a dying woman, and "ya flamin' mongrel" aimed at the listener turn the narrator coarse and hostile, which Wheeler never is.

flow.evidence: Clunky joins and broken words: "the bloody big flume stoushn't finished", "Anyway, why, it never made no difference", "dust'n raising", "rapt'n desperate".

variety.evidence: Many different interjections, but they are the same kind of tic each time: sentence-initial "Fair dinkum,", "Crikey,", "Jeez,", "Anyway," and tags "mate.", "cobber.".

essence.evidence: Recognisably the original because most of Twain's text is left in place ("Thish-yer Smiley had a mare"), but the bolted-on exclamations and the swearing make the narrator a different character.

problems.quote: the bloody big flume stoushn't finished
problems.why: 'stoushn't' is not a word; 'warn't' was mangled into stoush (a fight), breaking the sentence.

problems.quote: and if he couldn't he'd change sides, ya flamin' mongrel
problems.original: and if he couldn't he'd change sides
problems.why: Abuses the listener (a reverend) for no reason; changes the narrator's manner.
'Legend' is wrong sense for a pious, good parson and shifts the register to modern pub praise.
Swearing about the parson's dying wife jars with the solemn moment the joke depends on.
'Reckon' means to judge or suppose, not to pause and think; the sense is wrong.

problems.original: she get excited and desperate like

problems.why: Stock exclamation bolted onto the end, rendering nothing.

problems.quote: or somethin' of that kind, cobber
problems.why: Dated 'cobber' tag stuck on as decoration.

B.summary: Mostly the original with Aussie tokens sprinkled in; several wrong-sense swaps, a broken word, and bolted-on interjections and swearing that change the narrator.

meaning.evidence: Everything is there, in modern plain order: the dates, the flume, swapping sides, the birds, the straddle-bug, the parson's wife and the mare's finish. "taking the piss" for "only in fun" and "the arse end of the race" for "the fag end" keep the sense.

sense.evidence: Terms fit: "have a punt on it", "rolling in it or flat stony broke", "rocked up at the camp", "crook, real crook". "lucky as all get-out" is right in sense but American.

authenticity.evidence: Sounds like a real Australian telling it: "happy as Larry", "some other poor sod", "Smiley pipes up", "the mad bastard". "lucky as all get-out" is an American idiom left in.

register.evidence: Full yarn weight with uncle-bob swearing used naturally: "the lucky bastard", "taking the piss", "right at the arse end of the race", "some bloody thing". On the brief.

tone.evidence: The comic deadpan survives and the punchline "'Well, I'll put two and a half on her not making it, anyway.'" lands. The swearing is cheerful rather than hostile.

flow.evidence: Smooth, broken into speakable sentences: "Cat fight, he'd bet on it. Chook fight, he'd bet on it." Reads like it was told that way.

variety.evidence: Varied lexis ("bugger", "sod", "fella", "punt", "crook"), though "bloody" recurs: "any bloody thing", "no bloody difference", "some bloody thing", "every bloody time".

essence.evidence: Recognisably Jim Smiley's tale, but Twain's distinctive dialect ("curiousest", "warn't", "inf'nite", "Prov'dence") and the endless run-on sentence are normalised away: "thank the Lord for his infinite mercy". The garrulous voice remains, flattened a little.

problems.quote: he was lucky as all get-out
problems.why: 'As all get-out' is American, not Australian.

problems.quote: every bloody time she'd pull up at the stand
problems.original: always fetch up at the stand
problems.why: 'Bloody' is leaned on through the text (four or more times).

problems.quote: thank the Lord for his infinite mercy
problems.original: thank the Lord for his inf'nite mercy
problems.why: Normalising the dialect spellings loses some of the original's character.

C.summary: A fluent, natural, properly salty Aussie yarn that keeps every point; loses some of Twain's dialect texture and leans on 'bloody'.
